speaker: Vincent Clerc
title: The Potential of Data in Global Trade | Vincent Clerc
question: In international trade analytics, why can analysts estimate current global trade flows months before official statistics are published?
guest: There are a lot of new opportunities coming from transport data because in many aspects there is more, better, and earlier data available thanks to satellite tracking, especially of ships, than for the goods themselves. So we have worked on what we call a nowcast: you actually take shipping data and with this you forecast what will be reported as the trade statistics in two or three months from now, because the official trade statistics are not available today. They will be available in two, three, four months, or even longer depending on the country, since they are collected by customs. But we already know today at what speed which ship goes from where to where, thanks to satellite data.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Analysts can estimate trade flows early because trade leaves real-time digital traces long before customs agencies compile, reconcile, and publish official figures, which typically lag by weeks to months.

The most important source is ship-tracking data. Commercial vessels broadcast Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals giving their position, speed, and draught, which satellites and coastal receivers capture continuously. By combining port calls with changes in draught (how deep a ship sits, indicating how much cargo it carries) and vessel type and capacity, analysts infer volumes loaded and unloaded by port and country. The IMF's PortWatch and the Kiel Trade Indicator work this way.

These signals are supplemented by other high-frequency indicators: container throughput reported by ports, freight rates, air cargo data, bills of lading, purchasing managers' survey export orders, and early-reporting economies such as South Korea, whose 20-day export figures serve as a bellwether.

Statistical "nowcasting" models then map these timely indicators onto historical official data, exploiting their stable past relationships to produce estimates. These are approximations, since they capture volumes better than values and miss services trade, but they are reliable enough to reveal turning points early.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Official trade statistics rely on customs declarations, cross-border audits, and bureaucratic reconciliations, creating reporting lags of one to several months. Analysts bypass this delay through "nowcasting," which combines real-time physical movement data with high-frequency economic indicators. Because maritime transport carries roughly 80 percent of global merchandise trade by volume, satellite and terrestrial Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponders provide immediate visibility into ship locations, port calls, and vessel draft—how deeply a hull sits in the water, which reveals the weight of cargo loaded or unloaded.

Analysts enrich these maritime signals with air freight tracking, digital bills of lading, rail and road-toll telemetry, shipping rate indexes, satellite imagery of port and industrial activity, and survey-based Purchasing Managers’ Index export orders. Econometric and machine-learning models—such as those behind the IMF’s PortWatch and the Kiel Trade Indicator—calibrate these high-frequency physical and financial proxies against historical customs data. By mapping vessel types and routes to specific goods and price deflators, analysts translate raw transit activity into accurate estimates of global trade volumes and values months before official figures appear.

noweb.answer: Official trade statistics suffer from multi-month lags because governments must collect, audit, and reconcile millions of customs declarations. Analysts bypass this delay through "nowcasting," pairing econometric and machine-learning models with real-time data generated as goods physically move and transactions clear. A primary source is Automatic Identification System (AIS) satellite tracking, which continuously broadcasts cargo vessels' locations, speeds, and draft depths; by measuring how deeply ships sit in the water, analysts estimate cargo weights and port activity before goods ever clear customs. These maritime signals are combined with automated port container counts, air cargo tracking, digital bills of lading, and daily freight rates. Analysts further refine estimates using high-frequency commercial indicators, including export orders in purchasing managers' surveys, trade finance flows, and cross-border electronic payments. Because global supply chains follow established routes and historical value-to-weight relationships, models can synthesize these instantaneous logistical and financial footprints into accurate estimates of trade volumes and values months ahead of official releases.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Analysts can estimate trade months early because most goods leave a trail of real-time data long before customs agencies finish compiling and publishing official figures. The most important source is ship tracking. Cargo vessels broadcast their position, speed and draught through the Automatic Identification System (AIS). By combining those signals with vessel registries, analysts can work out port calls and roughly how much cargo was loaded or unloaded, almost as it happens. The IMF's PortWatch and UNCTAD's nowcasts use this approach.

They add other high-frequency indicators. These include container throughput at major ports, freight rates, air cargo volumes and the new export orders component of purchasing managers' surveys. Some countries also publish trade data unusually early, such as South Korea's exports for the first 10 and 20 days of each month, and these serve as bellwethers for global demand.

Nowcasting models, often statistical or machine-learning methods, combine these signals and are calibrated against past official data. That lets analysts estimate current trade flows weeks or months ahead of the official releases, which usually come out with a lag of one to three months or more.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer: Official international trade statistics take weeks or months to compile because customs agencies and national statistical offices must collect, classify, validate, and reconcile millions of declarations. Analysts bypass this lag by using real-time, high-frequency proxy data that capture the physical movement of goods as it happens. Most importantly, because maritime shipping carries roughly 80 percent of global merchandise trade by volume, analysts track Automatic Identification System (AIS) transponder signals from commercial vessels worldwide. Changes in a ship’s position, port calls, and draft—how deep the hull sits in the water—reveal when and roughly how much cargo is loaded or discharged. Analysts combine these maritime signals with satellite imagery of port congestion and container yards, electronic bills of lading, air cargo tracking, freight rate indices, and early port throughput reports. By feeding these near-real-time indicators into statistical and machine-learning nowcasting models calibrated against historical customs records, trade analysts can accurately estimate current global trade volumes and directional flows months before official government figures are released.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer: Analysts can estimate global trade months ahead of official releases because shipments leave digital traces as they happen. Vessel tracking signals, port calls, freight bookings, and customs filings available in some countries give early clues about what is moving, where it is going, and in what quantities. Analysts calibrate these signals against historical trade statistics to estimate current flows, a technique called nowcasting. Official figures take longer because statistical agencies must collect, check, and reconcile records across countries. Early estimates can therefore show where trade is headed, though they may be revised as fuller data arrive.
